cells.tense: You are here with the work, keeping it lit by attention, and you can feel it doing its job.
cells.ask: Let one person use something you've kept carefully made. Watch what happens when it goes back out.
cells.core:
You've built something through repetition. Not a flash of it, not a burst — the small light you keep lit because you show up to it. What change left behind, you've held onto and refined. And it's not brittle. You can pass a piece of it to someone else and not lose the shape of it.

That last part matters. Holding is one thing; holding and still being in exchange with people is another, and you're doing both. What this balance is free to feed next is fairness that flows both ways — giving what you've made and taking what comes back without counting it to death. Keeping it lit is already there. The exchange is the next thing it can carry.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it steady, and you can hand it on without losing it.
cells.verb: holding steady what the change already made
cells.place: in the small daily repetition that turns intention into skill

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future where the thing finally breaks, and the bracing has become its own practice.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're protecting and leave it completely alone for a day. See if it holds without you.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the work, guarding against a break that hasn't come. Every session becomes a chance to reinforce, to get ahead of the flaw, to make it unbreakable before it's even tested. The protecting has taken over the practice.

What this looks like going well is simpler: you keep the thing because it matters, and the mattering is felt, not defended. You started this because it connects you to someone, because the pull was there. That pull is what's being crowded out now. Holding on harder isn't the same as holding well. Let one thing be enough as it is for a day, and notice that the grip loosening is not the failure you've been bracing for.
cells.sheetLine: You built a fortress around something that was already holding.
cells.verb: holding steady what the change already made
cells.place: in the small daily repetition that turns intention into skill

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed, holding something you set down before that.
cells.ask: Do one small piece of the practice today — five minutes, no standard. Then say out loud what it's for.
cells.core:
The practice stopped, and whatever stopped it is behind you now, still taking up room. What came out of the change is still there — you haven't lost it — but it isn't being kept, and the small light isn't lit. You know what it would take to start again. That's not the missing piece.

What this looks like going well is a steady practice that keeps its own small light, refined by showing up, in exchange with no one but the work. What's missing now is direction from genuine engagement — movement from feeling, not from should. Not pushing yourself back into the old seat, but letting one honest step pull the rest through. What you made is intact. What went quiet is picking it back up.
cells.sheetLine: You still have what you made. You stopped picking it back up.

cells.tense: You are already keeping the shape of this steady, and you talk about it as if it holds itself.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've kept steady through your own attention and say, out loud, that you did that.
cells.core:
You're the one keeping this steady. The small daily repetition, the choices about what to protect and what to let shift — that's your hand on it. But when you describe it, it sounds like something that just happens, or that other people did.

What this looks like going well is structure that serves what it organizes — clear, reliable, things making sense because you made them so. That structure is already in motion. What's missing is the acknowledgment, not the work. You don't need to assert anything or dress it up. The authority is already running; it just hasn't been claimed by the person actually exercising it. Say it plain, to yourself, once. Let that be true.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one holding it steady. You haven't said so.

attempts.check: The record says what the card is, not what the person's history is; my drafts for Too Little and Unacknowledged must not name a former room, a person, or what was lost there, only locate the person without narrating the loss. A reader could reasonably say the mechanism language overreaches — that I cannot know their past — so all four cells describe a moment they could recognise rather than their story, and the ask stands on its own whether or not my read is right. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that flatters the capacity instead of handing the person something they can do today.
